body.text: Protests continued across the Philippines yesterday against the U.S. government’s Pax Silica initiative, ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump’s arrival in the country.

Over the past week, thousands of students, activists, indigenous community members, and others opposing Pax Silica have held protests in Metro Manila and other parts of the country, taking aim at the initiative’s potential social and environmental impact.

On Sunday, protesters clashed with police in Manila as they attempted to march on the Philippine International Convention Center, the venue of the 49th ASEAN Summit, leading to the arrest of around a dozen protesters. Another 276 people were arrested in Muntinlupa on the capital’s outskirts, as they prepared to march into central Manila to join the protests.

Demonstrations of various sizes continued across the country yesterday, with demonstrations taking place in Isabela, Baguio, and Batac City, in President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s home province of Ilocos Norte. In the latter location, protesters carried banners reading, “Trump Out! Reject Pax Silica!” and describing the U.S.-led economic and security initiative as a form of “imperialist plunder.” Another protest in Manila featured the slogan, “Get off our lands, we are not for sale.”

Pax Silica, which was launched last December, is intended to counter China’s control over the world’s supply of critical minerals, which the U.S. needs in order to secure its semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains. Twenty-six nations have signed up to the initiative so far, a number that Trump is hoping to increase during his brief stop in Manila for this week’s ASEAN meetings.

The first industrial hub to be constructed under Pax Silica is earmarked for a 4,000-acre economic security zone in New Clark City in Tarlac province on the island of Luzon, close to the former U.S. Clark Air Base. Its stated purpose is to “serve as a staging point for a purpose-built platform for allied manufacturing,” especially involving semiconductors, AI, and critical minerals.

The Philippine government estimates that the hub will attract up to $70 billion in investment and create up to 200,000 jobs, and the U.S. State Department claims that the agreement affirms the “shared commitment to advance mutual prosperity, technological progress, and economic security for our peoples.”

But Pax Silica has prompted widespread opposition in the Philippines. In August, more than 50 civil society groups came together to form the Network Opposed to Pax Silica, claiming that that the initiative will compromise Philippine sovereignty and is likely to have a series of serious social and environmental impacts.

The industrial zone in New Clark City is set to displace hundreds of indigenous Aeta people and local farmers in Tarlac province. Apung Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of an Aeta group in Sitio Sapang Kawayan in Tarlac, has described Pax Silica as “a violation of our rights, especially our community, our livelihood, our church, our burial ground,” according to Inquirer.net.
There have also been concerns about the hub’s gargantuan energy and water usage, as detailed by the New York Times yesterday:

Government estimates suggest that the project would require up to 90 million liters of water a day and 3 gigawatts of power. Its water needs would require amounts triple the area’s available supply during the dry season, while its projected power demand would be the equivalent of roughly a fifth of Philippine electricity consumption in 2024.

As the Times detailed, this has led to rumors that the hub will include a data center. While the Philippine government denies this, saying that it will mostly be focused on semiconductor manufacturing, the U.S. State Department said in a statement to the newspaper that this was yet to be determined.

For all of these reasons, the project has served as a flashpoint for anger over the overbearing influence of the United States, which ruled the Philippine islands as a colony for five decades and still retains considerable influence there. Since independence in 1946, the nation has seen frequent eruptions of nationalist anger against the U.S. presence. The issue figured heavily in the successful campaign for the closure of the giant U.S. military bases at Subic Bay and Clark in the early 1990s, and has raised its head periodically ever since.
“This is simply a new scheme where the U.S. will take control of the natural resources of our country,” Filipino Representative Antonio Tinio told CBS News.

While the current protests are a sign of the deep discontent that some Filipinos feel about the trajectory of relations with the U.S., there is little chance that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will pull out of Pax Silica or slow its implementation. After all, Philippine governments do not have a good track record of responding to grassroots activism on questions of social and environmental justice.

The more serious obstacle is domestic political realignments within the Philippines. The 2028 presidential election is likely to feature a showdown between the Marcos and Duterte families, who formed an alliance ahead of the 2022 election but have since experienced a bitter falling-out that has come to dominate the Philippines.

In a worrying sign for the country, the growing political enmity also tracks a growing polarization in terms of foreign policy, with Marcos favoring closer relations with the U.S. and his estranged vice president, Sara Duterte, expressing more skepticism about the relationship with Washington and a desire for better ties with Beijing.

While Duterte has so far not said much about Pax Silica, the possibility of another Duterte or a close ally in the Malacanang Palace probably poses the most serious long-term threat to the advance of Pax Silica in the Philippines.
